aspect_adaptations: All 10 aspects map directly onto C#; the adaptations are of mechanism, not of meaning: assertions_contracts is read against Debug.Assert being compiled out of Release builds (the C# analogue of Java's -ea model); memory_ownership is read as disposal ownership (IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable, one creator-disposer per resource) plus GC retention discipline (roots, caches, event handlers, rented buffers), since the GC owns reclamation; concurrency is read as async/Task discipline plus engine main-thread boundaries, which is where this estate's C# actually races.

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Microsoft's model is the guide's model: Debug.Assert is conditional on DEBUG and absent from Release, so it can only ever diagnose programmer invariants; boundary rejection belongs in explicit guard exceptions (ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull and siblings). Nullable flow analysis is static evidence, not a runtime boundary - Microsoft documents that deserialization/reflection can defeat it, as the guide states.
assertions_contracts.evidence: No .NET 10-era guidance changes assertion semantics or the ThrowIf* guard pattern; the guide's postconditions-are-tested-under-Release rule follows directly from the conditional-compilation fact.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: Debug.Assert for programmer invariants only - no mutation, authorization, or any needed side effect inside, because assertions are compiled out of Release. External input is rejected at the boundary with a precise exception (ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull, ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative, or a domain exception), guard clauses first so failure leaves state unchanged. Postconditions are documented and tested, including under Release configuration.

bounded_work.best_practice: No Microsoft source prescribes numeric budgets; nothing contradicts named bounds. The deferred-execution warning is core LINQ documentation behavior: an unmaterialized query re-runs per enumeration against possibly mutated state, which is why the guide's materialize-once-under-a-bound rule is the correct discipline.
bounded_work.evidence: Tiger policy stricter than mainstream by design; the guide names its bounds (ItemCountMax, PayloadSizeMaxBytes, DepthMax, MaxParallelism, retry count + shared deadline + backoff) and its reference module's executed cases (10 passed, per the commissioning record) exercise the count/total budgets at and past their limits.
bounded_work.guide_position: Every externally influenced size, count, duration, and fan-out gets a named PascalCase constant and a boundary rejection or clamp: item counts checked before allocation, byte payloads capped and streams read in bounded chunks (never ReadToEnd on untrusted length), every wait/retry/external call deadline-bound via CancellationToken, fan-out admitted through a bounded channel or semaphore, recursion over external data depth-capped. LINQ materializes once, at a named point, under a count bound. A retry without max attempts, shared deadline, and backoff is an unbounded loop.

concurrency.best_practice: Current Microsoft guidance is the guide's position: async all the way (blocking on .Result/.Wait() risks deadlock under a synchronization context and thread-pool starvation), ConfigureAwait(false) in library code with analyzer CA2007 enforcing it, CancellationToken flowed and honored, Task.Run reserved for CPU-bound offload, async void only for event handlers, ValueTask under its single-await consumption law.
concurrency.evidence: Nothing in the .NET 10 / C# 14 release changes async semantics in a way that relaxes any of these rules; the guide additionally handles the estate-specific boundary (engine coroutines/awaitables vs Task async crossed only at explicit adapters stating thread and cancellation owner), which platform guidance does not cover and does not contradict.
concurrency.guide_position: Async all the way to the entry point; never .Result, .Wait(), or .GetAwaiter().GetResult() outside a documented entry-point shim. One ConfigureAwait position per layer: libraries ConfigureAwait(false) (CA2007 under the house build), application/engine code captures its context deliberately. Every async API takes a CancellationToken last and honors it. Fire-and-forget is a decision with an owner (task stored, exceptions observed, lifetime bounded). lock regions are short, never span an await, and follow a stated order; shared mutable state has one owner and one stated discipline.

error_handling.best_practice: The guide's split is the documented idiom: exceptions for contract violations, TryX(out ...) for expected failures on hot/parsing paths, narrow catches, bare Exception only at top-level boundaries that log and translate, cause preserved (bare throw;, never throw ex;), and OperationCanceledException treated as control flow that propagates.
error_handling.evidence: No .NET 10 change alters exception or cancellation semantics; the async surfacing rule the guide documents (exceptions surface where the task is awaited) is the platform's stated behavior.
error_handling.guide_position: Contract violations throw precise exception types naming the rejected value's role (never secret content); expected failures return via TryX or a small result type. Catch only what the layer can interpret; empty catch forbidden; bare Exception only at a top-level boundary (process entry, engine callback root, message pump) that logs with context and translates or terminates by stated policy. Custom exceptions derive from Exception with standard constructors, sealed unless designed as a family base, few per subsystem.

formatting.best_practice: CSharpier is current at 1.3.0 (its latest release, which hardened XML formatting to error on syntax errors consistently with C#) and remains a Prettier-style opinionated re-printer - the property the guide's rationale rests on. dotnet format still normalizes per .editorconfig and does not re-wrap long lines, so the guide's division (CSharpier owns whitespace, dotnet format verifies style/analyzer rules in CI, never re-formats) is still the only way the pair holds the 100-column bound.
formatting.evidence: The belav/csharpier releases page (checked 2026-10-14) shows 1.3.0 as the current release; the guide names no CSharpier version of its own - the pin lives in each project's .config/dotnet-tools.json, so there is no guide-level version to go stale, and its documented-exception path (dotnet format + complete .editorconfig where the tool cannot be taken) is preserved.
formatting.guide_position: One formatter owns whitespace: CSharpier, pinned as a local dotnet tool in .config/dotnet-tools.json, configured in .csharpierrc.json with printWidth 100 and 4-space indentation stated explicitly; dotnet csharpier check is a gate. dotnet format runs in CI verify-only mode (--verify-no-changes) for the style/analyzer rules it owns and never reformats here. Two tools rewriting the same whitespace is forbidden; generated/engine files are excluded via .csharpierignore.

memory_ownership.best_practice: Adapted aspect: disposal ownership plus GC retention. Microsoft's guidance matches the guide's named failure modes - one long-lived HttpClient or IHttpClientFactory (per-call clients exhaust sockets), SafeHandle over hand-written finalizers, ArrayPool/MemoryPool rental with return on every path, and awareness of the ~85,000-byte large-object-heap threshold.
memory_ownership.evidence: No .NET 10 change to disposal, pooling, or LOH semantics contradicts any rule; the guide's engine carve-out (engine objects are not IDisposable and follow the engine's destroy discipline, kept separate from .NET disposal in code and comments) is an estate fact platform guidance does not address.
memory_ownership.guide_position: Whoever creates an IDisposable disposes it on every path (using / await using for IAsyncDisposable); ownership transfer is stated in the return documentation and visible in the API shape; disposal in own types is idempotent and safe on partially constructed objects. Retention is the leak model: event subscriptions pair += with -=, static fields and unbounded caches are roots with an eviction story, closures capturing this are named. Fast/large buffers rent from ArrayPool/MemoryPool and return on every path; hot structs stay small, with size assertions where per-frame/per-item counts are high.

security.best_practice: The guide's headline ban is now stronger than when such guides were first written: BinaryFormatter is obsolete as error (SYSLIB0011) and, since .NET 9, its runtime implementation is removed - the APIs throw for all project types, and Microsoft strongly recommends migrating away due to CWE-502 deserialization risk. Parameterized SQL, ArgumentList process launches, regex match timeouts, and XXE-safe XML settings (DtdProcessing prohibited, no external resolution) remain the documented controls.
security.evidence: Microsoft's own BinaryFormatter-removal post and the SYSLIB obsoletion index (checked 2026-10-14) confirm the guide's 'obsolete because unsafe-by-design' characterization and its ban; no current guidance relaxes the SQL, shell-string, or regex-timeout positions.
security.guide_position: Validate at the boundary, then trust inside - the boundary includes deserialization, reflection, P/Invoke, engine callbacks, and plugin/mod calls. Banned outright: BinaryFormatter and relatives, dynamic execution of external text, loading assemblies from untrusted paths without a stated trust decision. SQL parameterized always, including 'internal' queries. ProcessStartInfo with UseShellExecute=false and ArgumentList, never shell strings. unsafe blocks are small, commented with the invariant that makes them sound, and adversarially tested; P/Invoke crossings validate lengths, handles, and error codes. Secrets never in source, logs, exception messages, or fixtures.

static_analysis.best_practice: The house policy is the current Microsoft posture: nullable enabled from the first commit, TreatWarningsAsErrors in CI, AnalysisLevel at the current recommended level, EnforceCodeStyleInBuild with a committed .editorconfig, and XML docs on public APIs as a warning-level contract. The LSP pairing is also current: the Roslyn language server (Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.LanguageServer, the server the current VS Code C# extension is built on) is the ecosystem's center of gravity, with OmniSharp a fallback for legacy .NET Framework/Mono and script workloads.
static_analysis.evidence: The guide's OmniSharp characterization matches the project's own repo posture as cited in its Sources [C4]; netcoredbg (Samsung) remains the DAP debugger in the pairing at the 3.2.0-1092 release line the guide records. Vulnerability scanning via dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive is part of the guide's CI, matching current supply-chain practice.
static_analysis.guide_position: Shared build policy lives in Directory.Build.props (Nullable enable, LangVersion, TreatWarningsAsErrors at least in CI, AnalysisLevel current, EnforceCodeStyleInBuild); .editorconfig is committed and must agree with the formatter. A warning is a failed contract, not decoration; a public member without XML documentation is a warning and therefore an error in CI. Analyzers and source generators are pinned, reviewed dependencies whose output is treated as generated code.

testing.best_practice: xUnit v3 is the current xUnit.net feature line (the project shipped Core Framework v3 4.0.1 on 2026-09-12 and limits v2 to critical fixes); NUnit remains the runner Unity's Test Framework is built on, exactly the engine carve-out the guide makes. One runner per test project, async tests awaiting real operations under a test-level timeout, and deterministic tests (seeded randomness, TimeProvider fakes, no wall-clock sleeps) are current practice.
testing.evidence: xUnit.net's own release page (checked 2026-10-14) confirms the v3 line's currency; the guide's reference module mirrors its split in miniature (4 validation + 6 adversarial executed cases, per the guide text).
testing.guide_position: House runner for plain .NET is xUnit v3; NUnit where the engine's test framework dictates; one runner per test project. Half validation (contract holds: exactly-at-max admitted, designed null states, success postconditions, disposal on success path) / half adversarial (nulls where the type says never, deserializer-invented enum values, oversize/malformed payloads, cancellation mid-operation, disposal during use, concurrent callers, culture/time-zone shifts, double-returned rented buffers, unobserved faulted tasks). Engine tests split by host: pure logic tested engine-free, engine-hosted tests only for what needs the engine.

toolchain_pins.best_practice: The pins are the current official state: .NET 10 is the current LTS (released 2025-11-11, latest patch 10.0.12 of 2026-09-08, supported until 2028-11-14) and C# 14 is the default language version for net10.0 targets. .NET 8 (LTS) and .NET 9 (STS, now 24-month) both end support 2026-11-10, so the guide's 'existing .NET 8 projects are on a clock, new work does not start on STS' is about to become 'unsupported' on schedule. The next release, .NET 11, is an STS due November 2026 and not yet GA - it does not displace the LTS target.
toolchain_pins.evidence: Microsoft's official support-policy table and its .NET 8/9 end-of-support post (checked 2026-10-14) confirm every date the guide states: .NET 10 LTS to 2028-11-14, .NET 8 and .NET 9 both to 2026-11-10; Microsoft Learn's language-versioning table confirms net10.0 -> C# 14. SDK pinning via global.json with an explicit roll-forward policy remains the stated mechanism.
toolchain_pins.guide_position: Declare TFM, LangVersion, and SDK up front: net10.0 / C# 14 for plain .NET, LangVersion pinned explicitly (never latest or preview in shipped code), SDK pinned in global.json including roll-forward policy, nullable context part of the target declaration. Engine projects take their ceiling from the engine's compiler and record the engine version beside the pin. .NET 8 supported only until its 2026-11-10 end of support; runtime differences (JIT vs Native AOT vs Mono/IL2CPP) are put behind explicit boundaries and tested on the shipped runtime.

current_versions.csharp: C# 14, the default language version for net10.0 targets (Microsoft Learn language-versioning table); C# 15 arrives with the .NET 11 STS, not yet GA
current_versions.csharpier: 1.3.0 is the current release (belav/csharpier); the guide pins it per project in .config/dotnet-tools.json rather than naming a version in the guide
current_versions.dotnet: .NET 10 (LTS), released 2025-11-11, latest patch 10.0.12 (2026-09-08), supported until 2028-11-14. .NET 8 (LTS) and .NET 9 (STS) both end support 2026-11-10. .NET 11 (STS) is due November 2026 and is not a guide target
current_versions.netcoredbg: Samsung netcoredbg 3.2.0-1092 (June 2026) is the current release line per the guide's source [C5]; the DAP debugger in the pairing
current_versions.roslyn-ls: Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.LanguageServer (the Roslyn language server the current VS Code C# extension is built on) is the house LSP; OmniSharp is fallback-only for legacy .NET Framework/Mono and script workloads
current_versions.xunit: xUnit.net v3 is the current feature line (Core Framework v3 package 4.0.1, 2026-09-12; v2 limited to critical fixes); NUnit is the engine-hosted runner via Unity's Test Framework

proposals.evidence: Microsoft's end-of-support post confirms .NET 8 and .NET 9 receive no servicing updates, security fixes, or support after 2026-11-10 - less than a month after this audit - while .NET 10 LTS runs to 2028-11-14.
proposals.proposal: When .NET 8 crosses its 2026-11-10 end of support, revise the guide's section 2 wording from '.NET 8 supported until its end of support' (a future clock) to past tense with the migration expectation stated plainly, and drop .NET 8 from the header's supported line; .NET 11 (STS, due November 2026) should be named only as a non-target, like JDK STS releases in the sibling Java guide, unless the estate deliberately adopts it.
proposals.recommendation: Calendar for the first guide revision after 2026-11-10; no rule change, only currency wording.
